transcript.en: The university canteen must feed students a meal that meets nutrition targets at the lowest cost. Staff try menus by hand every week. A three-line model finds the best menu in milliseconds. How? Today: how linear programs model allocation problems, why the optimum sits at a corner, and how duality turns constraints into prices students can interpret. A linear program maximises or minimises a linear objective subject to linear constraints. The decision variables are continuous and usually non-negative. Diet, production and transport problems all fit this form. The constraints carve out a convex feasible region. Because the objective is linear, an optimum, if one exists, occurs at a vertex. The simplex method walks from vertex to better vertex until none is better. Evaluate three x plus two y at each vertex. The origin gives zero, the point four comma zero gives twelve, three comma one gives eleven, and zero comma two gives four. The optimum is twelve at four comma zero. Every linear program has a dual, with one variable per constraint. At the optimum, both have the same value. Each dual variable is a shadow price: how much the objective improves if that constraint is relaxed by one unit. Students often learn simplex tableaux as a ritual without seeing the geometry. Start with two-variable problems drawn on graph paper. Then let a solver handle larger ones, and spend the time interpreting shadow prices in context. Quick check! A linear program has a bounded, non-empty feasible region. Where must an optimal solution occur? At a vertex, or along an edge between two equally good vertices. That is why simplex only needs to visit corners. In the app, open the linear programming lab. Drag the objective line across the feasible region and watch where it last touches. Your turn. The oven-hours constraint has a shadow price of five. One more oven hour costs three. Should the canteen buy it? Yes: each extra hour adds five to the objective and costs three, a gain of two, while the price stays valid. Remember: optima sit at vertices, every LP has a dual, and shadow prices value constraints. Try it in your next lecture: give pairs a two-variable canteen problem on graph paper. They shade the feasible region, test every corner, and find the optimum. Then reveal the solver's shadow prices and ask what they mean for the manager.

body.en:
A linear program optimises a linear objective cᵀx subject to linear constraints Ax ≤ b and x ≥ 0. Dantzig’s simplex method (1947; Dantzig, 1963) exploits the geometry: the feasible region is a convex polyhedron, and if a finite optimum exists, one occurs at a vertex. Simplex moves between adjacent vertices, improving the objective at each step, and stops when no adjacent vertex is better. It is exponential in the worst case but fast in practice; interior-point methods (Karmarkar, 1984) run in polynomial time.

Every LP has a dual. For the primal max cᵀx s.t. Ax ≤ b, x ≥ 0, the dual is min bᵀy s.t. Aᵀy ≥ c, y ≥ 0. Weak duality says any feasible dual value bounds the primal; strong duality says the optimal values are equal; complementary slackness links which constraints bind to which dual variables are positive. Each optimal dual variable is a shadow price: the rate at which the objective improves per unit relaxation of its constraint, valid within a sensitivity range (Bertsimas and Tsitsiklis, 1997; Boyd and Vandenberghe, 2004).

Students commonly learn tableau pivoting as a ritual, believe the optimum may lie in the interior, round fractional answers, and cannot interpret dual values. Drawing two-variable problems first, sliding the objective line to the last vertex it touches, then using a solver for larger instances and spending the saved time on interpreting shadow prices and sensitivity in the problem’s own terms, builds the understanding that transfers.
body.ar:
يحسّن البرنامج الخطي دالة هدف خطية cᵀx تحت قيود خطية ⁦Ax ≤ b⁩ و⁦x ≥ 0⁩. وتستغل طريقة السمبلكس لـ Dantzig (١٩٤٧؛ Dantzig، ١٩٦٣) الهندسة: فالمنطقة الممكنة متعدد سطوح محدّب، وإذا وُجد أمثل محدود فإن أحدها يقع عند رأس. ويتنقل السمبلكس بين الرؤوس المتجاورة محسّنًا الهدف في كل خطوة، ويتوقف حين لا يكون أي رأس مجاور أفضل. وهو أُسّي في أسوأ الحالات لكنه سريع عمليًا، وتعمل طرق النقطة الداخلية (Karmarkar، ١٩٨٤) في زمن كثير حدود.

ولكل برنامج خطي ثنائي. فللبرنامج الأولي max cᵀx بحيث ⁦Ax ≤ b⁩ و⁦x ≥ 0⁩، يكون الثنائي min bᵀy بحيث Aᵀ⁦y ≥ c⁩ و⁦y ≥ 0⁩. وتنص الثنائية الضعيفة على أن أي قيمة ثنائية ممكنة تحد الأولي، وتنص الثنائية القوية على تساوي القيم المثلى، ويربط التراخي المتمم بين القيود المقيِّدة والمتغيرات الثنائية الموجبة. وكل متغير ثنائي أمثل هو سعر ظل: معدل تحسن الهدف لكل وحدة تخفيف في قيده، صالح داخل مدى حساسية (Bertsimas وTsitsiklis، ١٩٩٧؛ Boyd وVandenberghe، ٢٠٠٤).

وكثيرًا ما يتعلّم الطلاب الدوران في الجدول كطقس، ويعتقدون أن الأمثل قد يقع في الداخل، ويقرّبون الإجابات الكسرية، ولا يستطيعون تفسير القيم الثنائية. ورسم مسائل المتغيرين أولًا، وتحريك خط الهدف إلى آخر رأس يلمسه، ثم استخدام برنامج حل للحالات الأكبر وصرف الوقت الموفَّر في تفسير أسعار الظل والحساسية بلغة المسألة نفسها، يبني الفهم الذي ينتقل.

transcript.en: A model for the field-trip budget tells the faculty to hire two and a half buses. Rounding up breaks the budget, and rounding down leaves students behind. What should the model have said? Today: why many real decisions need whole numbers, why rounding a linear solution can fail badly, and how branch and bound finds proven optima. An integer program is a linear program in which some variables must be whole numbers. Yes-or-no decisions become zero-one variables. This small change makes the problem far harder in general. In the knapsack problem, each item has a weight and a value, and we choose items to maximise value within a capacity. The linear relaxation allows fractions of items. Its value is an upper bound on the true optimum. Here the relaxation happens to be whole, giving sixteen. But change the capacity to seven, and the relaxation picks a and two thirds of c, worth fourteen. Rounding down gives ten, yet b plus c gives thirteen. Branch and bound splits on a fractional variable, solving one branch with it set to zero and one with it set to one. Each relaxation gives a bound. Any branch whose bound is worse than the best whole solution found so far is pruned. Students tend to round linear solutions or believe the solver checks every combination. Draw the branch-and-bound tree for a four-item knapsack on the board. Let students compute each bound and decide which branches to prune. Quick check! The relaxation of a maximisation knapsack gives fourteen. What does that tell you about the integer optimum? It is at most fourteen. The relaxation has more freedom, so it can only do as well or better. Here the true optimum is thirteen. In the app, open the knapsack lab. Pick items by hand, compare with the relaxation, and watch branch and bound prune its tree. Your turn. The best whole solution so far is thirteen. A branch's relaxation gives twelve. What should branch and bound do? Prune it: nothing in that branch can beat thirteen. Remember: relaxations give bounds, rounding can be far from optimal, and branch and bound proves optimality by pruning. body.en:
Many decisions are indivisible: open a facility or not, assign an exam to a slot, hire a whole bus. Integer and mixed-integer programs add integrality to some variables, and binary variables encode logic such as either-or constraints and fixed costs. Integer programming is NP-hard in general, the 0–1 knapsack being among Karp’s (1972) classic NP-complete problems, though it admits a pseudo-polynomial dynamic program in O(nW).

The LP relaxation, dropping integrality, gives a bound: for maximisation, the relaxation’s value is at least the integer optimum. Rounding a relaxed solution can be infeasible or far from optimal. Branch and bound (Land and Doig, 1960) solves the relaxation, picks a fractional variable, and branches into subproblems with that variable fixed; each subproblem’s relaxation bounds everything below it, and any node whose bound cannot beat the best integer solution found so far, the incumbent, is pruned. The gap between bound and incumbent certifies solution quality even when the search stops early. Modern solvers add cutting planes, presolve and heuristics (Wolsey, 2020).

Students tend to round, to believe solvers enumerate all combinations, and to ignore formulation strength. Drawing a small branch-and-bound tree by hand, computing each bound and pruning decision, then comparing a weak and a strong formulation of the same problem on a solver, makes the ideas concrete and shows why good formulations matter as much as good algorithms.

transcript.en: The faculty must schedule six hundred exams into three weeks with no student sitting two at once. An exact solver runs all weekend and does not finish. A simple heuristic finds a clash-free timetable in a minute. Is it the best one? Today: why some problems are too large for exact methods, how local search gets stuck, and how simulated annealing escapes by sometimes accepting worse moves. Many scheduling and routing problems are NP-hard, so exact methods may take impossibly long on large instances. Heuristics trade the guarantee of optimality for good solutions found quickly. They need careful evaluation instead. Local search starts from a solution and repeatedly moves to a better neighbour, for example by moving one exam to another slot. It stops when no neighbour is better. That point is a local optimum, which may be far from the best. Simulated annealing sometimes accepts a worse move, with probability e to the minus delta over T. At high temperature it explores freely. As T cools, it settles, and with slow enough cooling it can escape local optima. A move that is worse by two is accepted with probability e to the minus two at temperature one, about fourteen percent. At temperature ten it is accepted about eighty two percent of the time. Cooling turns exploration into refinement. Students often report one run of a heuristic and call it the answer. Require several runs with different seeds, a comparison with a lower bound or an exact solution on small instances, and a plot of cost against time. Quick check! Local search stops with eight clashes left, and no single exam move reduces them. What has it found? A local optimum. No neighbour is better, but a sequence of moves, some worse at first, might reach zero clashes. In the app, open the annealing lab. Run local search and annealing on the same problem, change the cooling rate, and compare the final costs. Your turn. At temperature two, how likely is annealing to accept a move that is worse by two? About thirty seven percent: e to the minus one. Remember: local search finds local optima, annealing escapes by accepting some worse moves, and heuristics must be evaluated over many runs. Try it in your next lecture: give each row of students a different random seed and the same timetable problem. Each row runs annealing and reports its final cost. Plot all the results on the board and discuss the spread.

body.en:
Timetabling, vehicle routing and many scheduling problems are NP-hard, and realistic instances can be too large for exact methods within the time available. Heuristics and metaheuristics trade optimality guarantees for good solutions quickly. Local search starts from a solution and moves to improving neighbours defined by a move, such as reassigning one exam; it stops at a local optimum, which depends on the start and on the neighbourhood.

Simulated annealing (Kirkpatrick, Gelatt and Vecchi, 1983), inspired by the Metropolis criterion, accepts a worsening move of size Δ with probability e^(−Δ/T), where the temperature T is lowered by a cooling schedule. At high T the search explores; as T falls it refines. With sufficiently slow logarithmic cooling it converges to a global optimum in probability, but practical schedules, typically geometric, carry no guarantee. Tabu search, genetic algorithms and large neighbourhood search are related alternatives; the no-free-lunch theorems (Wolpert and Macready, 1997) warn that no method dominates across all problems.

Because heuristics are stochastic and unguaranteed, evaluation is the core skill. Students should run several seeds and report distributions, compare against exact optima on small instances or against lower bounds on large ones, plot cost against time, and tune parameters on instances separate from those used for final comparison. Classroom experiments where each group runs a different seed make variability visible and discourage reporting a single lucky run.

الجدولة الزمنية وتوجيه المركبات ومسائل جدولة كثيرة صعبة من نوع NP، وقد تكون الحالات الواقعية أكبر من أن تحلها الطرق الدقيقة في الوقت المتاح. وتتنازل الطرق التقريبية والطرق فوق التقريبية عن ضمانات الأمثلية مقابل حلول جيدة سريعة. ويبدأ البحث المحلي من حل ويتنقل إلى جيران أفضل تحددهم نقلة، مثل إعادة تعيين امتحان واحد، ويتوقف عند قمة محلية تتوقف على نقطة البداية وعلى الجوار.

ويقبل التلدين المحاكى (Kirkpatrick وGelatt وVecchi، ١٩٨٣)، المستوحى من معيار Metropolis، نقلة مسيئة بمقدار Δ باحتمال ⁦e^(−⁩Δ/T)، حيث تُخفَّض درجة الحرارة T بجدول تبريد. فعند T المرتفعة يستكشف البحث، ومع انخفاضها يحسّن. ومع تبريد لوغاريتمي بطيء بما يكفي يتقارب احتماليًا إلى الأمثل العام، لكن الجداول العملية، الهندسية عادة، لا تحمل أي ضمان. والبحث المحظور والخوارزميات الجينية والبحث في الجوار الواسع بدائل ذات صلة، وتحذّر مبرهنات لا غداء مجاني (Wolpert وMacready، ١٩٩٧) من أنه لا توجد طريقة تتفوق في كل المسائل.

ولأن الطرق التقريبية عشوائية وبلا ضمان، يصبح التقييم المهارة الجوهرية. فينبغي أن يشغّل الطلاب عدة بذور ويعرضوا التوزيعات، ويقارنوا بالأمثل الدقيق في الحالات الصغيرة أو بالحدود الدنيا في الكبيرة، ويرسموا التكلفة مقابل الزمن، ويضبطوا المعاملات على حالات منفصلة عن تلك المستخدمة في المقارنة النهائية. وتجارب القاعة التي تشغّل فيها كل مجموعة بذرة مختلفة تُظهر التباين وتثبّط عرض تشغيلة واحدة محظوظة.

transcript.en: A student team's model of the campus shuttle cut cost by thirty percent. The transport office rejected it at once: it left the night students with no bus. The solver was right. The model was not. Why? Today: why formulating a model is the hardest skill in optimisation, how to teach the modelling cycle, and how to assess models rather than just answers. An optimisation model has decision variables, an objective and constraints. Choosing them is a judgement about the real problem. A missing constraint lets the solver exploit a loophole, just as a missing rule lets an agent game its reward. Modelling is a cycle, not a single step. Understand the problem with stakeholders, formulate, solve, then validate the solution against reality. When validation fails, as with the night buses, return and revise. The fix is one line: every route must have at least one bus in every time period with demand. With it, the cost saving drops to eighteen percent, and the office accepts the model. Textbook exercises hand students the variables. Real work starts from a vague brief. Give students a short messy brief and a stakeholder to interview, and make them state every assumption. If you grade only the optimal value, students learn to chase numbers. Grade the formulation, the stated assumptions, validation against the brief, and a sensitivity analysis. A short oral defence shows who understands the model. Quick check! The solver found the true optimum of the students' model, yet the plan was rejected. Which stage of the modelling cycle failed? Formulation: a real requirement was left out. Validation with the transport office caught it, and the cycle sent the team back to revise. In the app, open the modeller lab. Turn a short brief into variables, an objective and constraints, solve it, and check the answer against the brief. Your turn. Two teams report the same optimal cost. What best shows which team modelled the problem well? Their stated assumptions, validation against the brief, and how they defend the model orally. Remember: modelling is a cycle, validation catches missing constraints, and assessment should reward the model, not just the number. Try it in your next lecture: read a four-sentence brief about the campus shuttle and play the transport officer. Teams interview you for ten minutes, then write variables, objective and constraints. Reveal the night-bus requirement only to teams who ask.

body.en:
Solvers are now powerful and accessible, so the bottleneck in applied optimisation is formulation: choosing decision variables, an objective and constraints that capture what stakeholders actually need. Williams’s Model Building in Mathematical Programming describes modelling as an iterative cycle of problem understanding, formulation, solution, validation and revision. A model that omits a real requirement will be solved perfectly and rejected in practice, exactly as an agent with a mis-specified reward games it.

Research on mathematical modelling education (Blum and Leiß, 2007) identifies the transitions in the cycle, from situation to model and from mathematical result back to the situation, as where students struggle most. Textbook exercises usually hand students the variables, skipping the hardest step. Open, messy briefs, interviews with a real or role-played stakeholder, explicit assumption lists, and validation against the brief all build this competence. Sensitivity analysis, asking how the solution changes when data or assumptions change, links back to shadow prices and builds judgement.

Assessment must reward the model rather than the number. Rubrics should weight the formulation and its justification, stated assumptions, validation and sensitivity, and communication to a non-specialist, with a short oral defence to confirm understanding. Two teams can report the same optimal value with very different models, and only examination of the model reveals which would survive contact with the real problem.

أصبحت برامج الحل قوية ومتاحة، فصار عنق الزجاجة في التحسين التطبيقي هو الصياغة: اختيار متغيرات القرار ودالة الهدف والقيود التي تلتقط ما يحتاجه أصحاب المصلحة فعلًا. ويصف كتاب Williams بناء النماذج في البرمجة الرياضية النمذجةَ دورةً تكرارية من فهم المسألة والصياغة والحل والتحقق والمراجعة. والنموذج الذي يُغفل متطلبًا حقيقيًا سيُحل بإتقان ويُرفض عمليًا، تمامًا كما يتلاعب وكيل بمكافأة محددة خطأً.

وتحدد أبحاث تعليم النمذجة الرياضية (Blum وLeiß، ٢٠٠٧) الانتقالات في الدورة، من الموقف إلى النموذج ومن النتيجة الرياضية عودةً إلى الموقف، بوصفها أكثر ما يتعثر فيه الطلاب. وتعطي تمارين الكتب المدرسية الطلاب المتغيرات عادة، متجاوزة أصعب خطوة. وتبني هذه الكفاءة الأوصافُ المفتوحة غير المرتبة، والمقابلات مع صاحب مصلحة حقيقي أو ممثَّل، وقوائم الافتراضات الصريحة، والتحقق مقابل الوصف. ويربط تحليل الحساسية، أي سؤال كيف يتغيّر الحل حين تتغيّر البيانات أو الافتراضات، بأسعار الظل ويبني الحكم.

ويجب أن يكافئ التقييم النموذج لا الرقم. فينبغي أن تزن معايير التقييم الصياغة وتبريرها، والافتراضات المعلنة، والتحقق والحساسية، والتواصل مع غير المتخصص، مع دفاع شفهي قصير لتأكيد الفهم. فقد يعلن فريقان القيمة المثلى نفسها بنموذجين مختلفين جدًا، ولا يكشف أيّهما سيصمد أمام المسألة الحقيقية إلا فحص النموذج.
